'''Mamoru "Mark" Mohri''', {{post-nominals|country=AUS|size=100|post-noms=[[Honorary Member of the Order of Australia|AM]]}} ({{langx|ja|毛利 衛|Mōri Mamoru}}; born 29 January 1948) is a Japanese scientist, a former [[National Space Development Agency of Japan|NASDA]] astronaut, and a veteran of two [[NASA]] [[Space Shuttle]] missions. He is the first Japanese astronaut who was part of an official Japanese space program. The first Japanese person in space, [[Toyohiro Akiyama]], was a journalist who was trained in the Soviet Union.

==Biography==
Born in [[Yoichi, Hokkaidō]], Japan, Mohri earned both a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] and [[Master of Science|MSc]] degree in chemistry from [[Hokkaido University]] in respectively 1970 and 1972, and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree in chemistry from [[Flinders University]] in [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], in 1976.<ref>[https://iss.jaxa.jp/shuttle/flight/sts99/pdf/leaflet_hi.pdf The Earth "MAHOROBA" - Astronaut Mohri's STS-99 Earth Observation Mission] - website of [[JAXA]]</ref>

Most of Mohri's work has been in the field of [[Materials science|materials]] and [[vacuum]] [[science]]s. From 1975 to 1985, Mohri was a member of the [[nuclear engineering]] [[faculty (teaching staff)|faculty]] of Hokkaido University, where he worked on [[nuclear fusion]]-related projects.

==Astronaut career==
Mohri was selected by the [[Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency|National Space Development Agency of Japan]] (now [[JAXA]]) to train as a [[Payload Specialist|payload specialist]] for a Japanese materials science payload. He flew his first space mission aboard [[STS-47]] in 1992 as chief payload specialist for [[Spacelab#Spacelab missions|Spacelab-J]]. Mohri subsequently made another trip into space as part of mission [[STS-99]] in 2000.

As of 2001, Mohri is the Chief Executive Director Emeritus for the [[Miraikan]], the [[National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation]] in Tokyo.

==Honours==
On 16 March 2006 Mohri was appointed an Honorary Member of the [[Order of Australia]] (AM), “for service to Australia-Japan education and science relations.”<ref>[https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1129458 It's an Honour] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190222042024/https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1129458 |date=22 February 2019 }}. Itsanhonour.gov.au (2006-03-16). Retrieved on 2011-06-24.</ref>
